title: DNS, TCP, TLS & HTTPS
summary: Follow a browser request from a domain name to a secure connection: DNS finds the server, TCP carries data, and TLS protects it.

subtopics.title: Website name lookup
subtopics.explanation: DNS helps a browser find the network address behind a website name. The browser or operating system may already have a cached answer. If not, the lookup travels through a resolver before the request begins. It is like checking an address book before sending a letter. For example, a first visit may wait for a DNS answer that later visits reuse from a cache. For example, a repeated page visit may reuse a cached DNS answer.

subtopics.title: TCP connection
subtopics.explanation: TCP opens a reliable connection between the browser and server. It numbers data and checks that missing pieces are sent again. A new connection can require extra network trips, especially on distant networks. Think of it as agreeing on a delivery route before moving the boxes. For example, a new connection can add delay before any page bytes arrive. For example, a new TCP connection can add delay before the request is sent.

subtopics.title: TLS protection
subtopics.explanation: TLS creates an encrypted connection and checks that the server has a certificate for the requested site. Encryption makes it harder for others on the route to read or alter data. HTTPS uses HTTP over this protected connection. A checked badge helps identify the right shop. For example, a browser checks the certificate name while establishing a protected connection. For example, check the certificate name when diagnosing an HTTPS warning. TLS is like sealing a letter and checking the recipient address while it travels.

subtopics.title: HTTP request
subtopics.explanation: After connecting, the browser sends an HTTP request for a page or file. It includes a method and address, and may include headers or a body. The server replies with a status and content. This is like asking a clerk for one item and receiving a labeled package. For example, the HTTP response can contain HTML that refers to more assets. For example, the browser may make later requests for assets referenced by the HTML response.

subtopics.title: Latency
subtopics.explanation: Each network trip takes time, even when the amount of data is small. DNS lookup, connection setup, and server response all affect how quickly content arrives. Reuse connections and reduce unnecessary requests. Fewer trips are like fewer stops on a delivery route. For example, measure the number and distance of network round trips when a page feels slow. For example, use network timing to distinguish lookup time from server response time.

foundations.overview: Before a webpage loads, the browser must find a server and connect to it safely. DNS finds the address; TCP carries the conversation; TLS protects it. HTTPS is HTTP using that protected connection. Think of ordering a parcel: find the address, establish delivery, then seal the package.
foundations.formalDefinition: DNS resolves domain names to IP addresses. TCP provides an ordered, reliable byte stream. TLS provides encryption and server authentication. HTTPS is HTTP transported over TLS.
foundations.whyItMatters: DNS, TCP, and TLS contribute separate setup steps before page data arrives. Distinguishing them makes performance and connection-security issues easier to investigate.
foundations.mentalModel: Finding a server is like looking up an address. TCP is the delivery route. TLS seals and verifies the message.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser coordinates DNS, connection setup, HTTPS, HTTP requests, caching, and rendering. Browser tools show timings for each part of this journey.
foundations.realWorldUsage: When a site fails, check whether name lookup, certificate setup, server response, or a later asset request is failing.
foundations.businessImpact: Fast, secure connections make pages feel dependable, especially for returning visitors and users far from the server.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Separate connection delays from slow server work before changing application code.
foundations.performanceImpact: Reuse connections, serve assets from nearby edges, and reduce avoidable network round trips.
commonUseCases: Troubleshooting a site that cannot connect

commonMisconceptions.myth: HTTPS means the website itself is trustworthy
commonMisconceptions.reality: HTTPS protects the connection; it does not prove every site is honest.

commonMisconceptions.myth: DNS runs again for every file
commonMisconceptions.reality: DNS results can be cached and reused for later requests.

commonMisconceptions.myth: TLS encrypts data after it reaches the server.
commonMisconceptions.reality: TLS protects data in transit between endpoints; application code must still protect stored data.

commonMisconceptions.myth: DNS lookup always happens for every request.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Resolvers and browsers can cache answers according to DNS settings and time limits.

keyTakeaways: DNS helps a browser find the network address behind a website name.
TCP opens a reliable connection between the browser and server.
TLS creates an encrypted connection and checks that the server has a certificate for the requested site.
